title: Mandelson kept lobby firm shares for months as US ambassador despite conflict of interest fears, documents show
description: Lord Mandelson still held shares in his lobbying company eight months after becoming US ambassador, despite government concens about conflicts of inte
body: Lord Mandelson still held shares in his lobbying company eight months after becoming US ambassador, despite government concens about conflicts of interest, newly released documents show.The peer was sacked as ambassador last year by Sir Keir Starmer following revelations about the extent of his relationship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.This 85-page release is the third since MPs voted to publish documents aiming to reveal behind-the scenes-discussions about how he was appointed to the role.The documents were previously withheld due to the Metropolitan Police investigation into allegations Lord Mandelson had passed market-sensitive government information to Epstein.Sir Olly Robbins was sacked as head of the Foreign Office by Sir Keir Starmer during the scandal when it emerged Lord Mandelson had been granted clearance for the role despite concerns being raised by vetting officials.The newly released documents highlight that Lord Mandelson was able to keep his shares in Global Counsel, the lobbying company he co-founded, while serving as ambassador to Washington.They reveal civil servants' concerns about the risk of perceived conflict of interest. But selling the shares was clearly not a condition of him taking up the role.Part of that is because of the desire in Sir Keir's government at the time to have Lord Mandelson in Washington as quickly as possible. That is exemplified in an email from Sir Olly, saying a process to police Mandelson's conflicts of interest could be "up and running in a light touch way".Another factor is selling shares in a private company like Global Counsel requires finding a new buyer or selling them back to the company.But the documents also reveal Lord Mandelson had not sold his shares back to Global Counsel because their offer was not the "fair value". Another attempt to sell to a different buyer fell through.The result was Mandelson kept his shares, and while in office tried to set up a meeting between Global Counsel and a key Donald Trump advisor, as well as taking the firm's advice on a speech on Britain's role in the world.Lord Mandelson remained a shareholder until February 2026, the same month the company went into administration.Emails about his dealings with his Washington counterparts show a close relationship, with one message from an unnamed White House official in April 2025 telling Lord Mandelson his label as the "Prince of Darkness" could not be "farther from the truth".Ahead of  a speech he was due to give on Britain's role "in the age of Trump", documents show him seeking advice from a Global Counsel employee in August 2025, during his time as ambassador.The exchange contains feedback from an unnamed Global Counsel director, who suggested he should use "warmer language" about China and tone down "parts of your apologia of the Trump administration".The director warned: "Scepticism of [the Trump administration] is now so deep – at least in the public policy-interested world outside government – that it would be counterproductive/unpersuasive if you came across as having drunk the Kool Aid."Lord Mandelson responds to say he would water down his language, and in another email tries to arrange an "under the radar" lunch meeting to discuss China and trade between a GC employee and someone from the US President's Council of Economic Advisers. On the domestic front, Lord Mandelson also sent texts to Sir Keir's then chief of staff Morgan McSweeney in September 2025 offering advice on a cabinet reshuffle. He suggested moving Darren Jones to lead the science and technology department as a way to "solve your Darren issue", although McSweeney did not respond until after the reshuffle decisions had been made, with Jones given a newly-created role as chief secretary to the prime minister.Lord Mandelson has yet to comment on the most recent release of papers relating to his appointment. He has repeatedly let it be known he believes he has not acted criminally, did not act for personal gain and is cooperating with the police. No charges have been made. A Met Police spokesperson told the BBC: "Our investigation into alleged misconduct in public office is ongoing."Speaking to journalists in the Downing Street garden following the release of the documents, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would address culture change for Westminster as part of his 10 year plan, which he said will be published next month.He said: "I've come back in as something of an outsider into the system and I see a lot of things that I think need to change to improve the political culture of this country and to strengthen the public interests when it comes to all of these issues."Security minister Dan Jarvis told MPs: "The government recognises that action needs to be taken in response to the issues raised by Mandelson's appointment."He said action had already been taken to strengthen the vetting and appointments process, including strengthening the management of conflicts of interest.Future appointments will not be made before security clearance has been granted, he said, adding that review by Sir Adrian Fulford of vetting procedures was nearing completion.A separate review by Sir Anthony Finkelstein into use of personal messaging services including WhatsApp and Signal for business purposes is expected to be published in January next year.

schema.headline: Mandelson kept lobby firm shares for months as US ambassador despite conflict of interest fears, documents show

title: When will Poundland shops close? Five key questions answered
description: This is the question that is most difficult to answer. Poundland shops will remain open as usual for now. The firm collapsing has acted as a reset in
body: This is the question that is most difficult to answer. Poundland shops will remain open as usual for now. The firm collapsing has acted as a reset in the process of selling it.Administrators are looking to either sell the business as a whole, or to break it up, which is the more likely outcome.When Poundland was still a going concern, Irish property firm Martin Property Group made an offer for it. But a source said the group was now "unlikely" to make a fresh bid due to "irreparable harm" to the brand from the administration process.Before the collapse, Fortress, which owns rival budget chain Poundstretcher, was interested in buying about 200 of the stores, and wanted to keep those trading under the Poundland brand.But Fortress's position at the moment is unclear. The BBC understands it is considering selling Poundstretcher, a move first reported by Bloomberg.A decision on Poundstretcher could come before the end of this week. However, Fortress has declined to comment.That depends on who you ask.When the chain was sold by Pepco last year for £1 it was struggling. It suffered a £68m loss that year.Poundland's managing director Barry Williams said Poundland had been seeing a "strong recovery". In the year to this September it recorded a profit of £18.1m. Sales were up 3.3% going into the vital Christmas period.Poundland's management paint a picture of a retailer that was turning a corner until the owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, pulled the plug on funding for day-to-day expenses such as buying stock.The Usdaw union, which represents shopworkers, claim the owners forced Poundland into administration.Labour MP Antonia Bance said she was "pretty appalled" by the conduct of Gordon Brothers over the past few weeks, and that it was going to make much bigger profits by breaking up the business rather than by keeping it going.However, Gordon Brothers insisted the business was not turning a profit, and had missed budget forecasts.A spokeswoman said while the management team had made £100m in cost reductions, the business had moved from a £70m loss to "around break-even" on paper."Break-even is different from generating the cash needed to buy stock, invest, and withstand increasing economic pressures," the spokeswoman said. "A few good weeks do not make a turnaround."Poundland repeatedly missed budget targets over the year, the spokeswoman added.Gordon Brothers was concerned that as inflation goes up next year, those pressures would have helped to make the business unviable, it said.And Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency agency Begbies Traynor, said Poundland's collapse "seemed somehow inevitable" due to challenges facing retailers - including higher costs to employ staff.Stores are still trading while the administrators work out if the business is viable. The funds locked up by Gordon Brothers - at the last count about £70m - have now been released by the administrators.This has turned the taps back on, so staff will continue to be paid in the run-up to Christmas, and so will suppliers.But here's the catch: the administrators have a legal obligation to maximise value for "secured" creditors. It means the owners, Gordon Brothers, are at the head of the queue for being paid back the loans that were stumbling blocks in the negotiations.But more importantly for staff, if the administrators can get more value by breaking up the business than by selling it as a whole, then that is what they have to do, even if the business would be viable.If the business is broken up and its stores are sold off, the new owners would not be obliged to keep staff on. That depends on what happens next.Administrators will have to get the best value for creditors, which could mean selling the business as it stands.But if Poundland is broken up, administrators could sell the brand without the stores, or the brand along with some of the stores, or the stores without the Poundland brand, to other retailers.As a result there could be fewer discount stores on the High Street, providing less incentive for other retailers to keep prices down."Poundland is a place they go on the High Street to get bargains and... given the cost of living challenges we face, that is of concern to us in government," Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, told the BBC on Thursday.Poundland's customers may well turn to rival budget retailers in the hunt for bargains.

schema.headline: When will Poundland shops close? Five key questions answered

title: UK reservists contacted as 'threat environment' rises, Streeting says
description: The Ministry of Defence has written to ex-military personnel to check their contact details and skills against the backdrop of a rising "threat enviro
body: The Ministry of Defence has written to ex-military personnel to check their contact details and skills against the backdrop of a rising "threat environment", Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has said.It comes after The Times and the Telegraph reported that reservists who previously served in the Armed Forces have received letters telling them to prepare to be called up for war.Streeting told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that this meant should they ever be needed  "either for a national disaster here at home or for a more serious threat or conflict elsewhere" then they would "know where our strategic reserve is" and what their skills were."I want the country to be alert, not alarmed," he said. "You can't not look at what's going on in Europe and not be concerned about a threat environment which has deteriorated in recent years and is sadly increasing," Streeting told Today."We saw last Friday a very serious incident – the incursion into Polish airspace by Russian missiles, we've seen state-sponsored terrorism waged by Russia across Europe, we've obviously had incidents concerning Iran around RAF bases here in the UK."And so against that backdrop, against that threat environment, the government and the country has to be ready to face down those risks."He added: "Because the more ready we are the less likely we are to find ourselves in a conflict, in a war, that is my goal, that is the goal of this government."Streeting told BBC Breakfast that "if, God forbid, this country did find itself at war" and there was then an inquiry, the Ministry of Defence would be criticised if the government had not kept its records up-to-date."The Telegraph reported that the letters offered opportunities to volunteer, external for training and exercises.This is not a case of pressing the panic button for imminent war, but more one of good housekeeping.When Britain went to war in Iraq in 2003 the MoD had a poor grasp of who might be available to serve, what current skills they had and what their up-to-date contact details were. So they obviously don't want to be in that situation if there is a national crisis in the future that triggers a mobilisation.Twenty three years on, the Ukraine war has changed everything. It's brought a hot war to the very borders of Nato, it's exposed the dangers of having too few troops available, but most of all it has changed the nature of warfare.People who have spent their adult lives never touching a weapon can turn out to be extraordinarily skilled drone operators, those with a talent for electronics, radio and signals work have a vital role to play in electronic warfare. So this exercise by the government, probably long overdue, is about knowing who can do what and where they can be contacted.Justin Crump, a former Army officer and now CEO of the business intelligence firm Sibylline, told the BBC: "Ukraine has shown us the importance of mobilising civilian skills and approaches in modern warfare. This is a first step, and an overdue one in many ways, with the effort likely to increase through early 2027. [It is] very much a part of deterrence and not an intention to use people".He said veterans - a sometimes misleading term for men and women who are often in peak physical shape and fitness - that he has contacted have generally responded positively to the move. "After all", he said, "they signed up to help before, but want to make sure their enhanced skills and talents are valued".The MoD's decision to contact ex-military personnel comes after news that the UK has signed an £8bn contract to upgrade its nuclear submarine fleet, which the defence secretary said would help get the country "warfighting ready".Meanwhile, Streeting also praised the Duke of Sussex's "patriotic spirit" after the former soldier said he would rejoin the armed forces again if needed.Asked whether there could be a role for Harry, the defence secretary told Today: "I'm always happy to talk to him about how we can work together, whether that's through his Invictus Games, which does a brilliant job supporting our veterans and giving them opportunities to take part in those amazing and inspiring competitive sporting events, but he does have experience to bring to bear."Streeting praised the "service he's given to our country" and the fact he had spoken about his "willingness and readiness to serve"."I think that's exactly the sort of patriotic spirit we're looking for," he said."I think it's that sort of patriotic spirit we'll find throughout our strategic reserve."Last week, Harry, who spent a decade in the forces and served on the front line in Afghanistan, said: "If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country, alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel."

schema.headline: UK reservists contacted as 'threat environment' rises, Streeting says

title: Nearly 100 Labour MPs including ministerial aides oppose Rosebank oil field
description: Ministerial aides are among nearly 100 Labour MPs who have signed a letter to the prime minister to express their opposition to the Rosebank oil field
body: Ministerial aides are among nearly 100 Labour MPs who have signed a letter to the prime minister to express their opposition to the Rosebank oil field.The government could also face resignations from junior ranks if the project goes ahead, the BBC has been told.Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is due to make a decision on whether to give the go-ahead for drilling in the oil field off the north-west coast of Shetland within weeks.The government has remained tight-lipped - both publicly and privately - about what it is likely to do.Those close to the energy secretary insist that she has not yet made her decision.But 92 Labour MPs have signed a letter, sent to the prime minister today, urging him not to allow the project to go ahead. Ministerial aides - the most junior rank of government - are among the signatures.The MP who organised the letter, Catherine Fookes, said: "If Rosebank is approved, champagne corks will pop in the offices of oil companies - but it will not make an iota of difference to my constituents' energy bills. "The oil belongs to private companies, and will only be shipped overseas to the highest bidder."What it will do, however, is accelerate the climate crisis, which is already pushing up food bills, causing devastating winter floods like those we saw in Monmouthshire last year, and fuelling wildfires across our green landscapes in summer."It's the most visible demonstration yet of the deep divides in the Labour Party over the issue.The decision about whether to approve Rosebank involves a legal process which technically lies solely with the energy secretary.Fahnbulleh has, in the past, been regarded as someone personally opposed to the oil field.Others in the cabinet, including Chancellor John Healey, have let it be known that they would like to see the project given the go-ahead; while the prime minister has repeatedly said he wants to take a "pragmatic" approach to North Sea oil and gas.But Fahnbulleh insisted last month that she alone would make the final decision and claimed the courts would ultimately side with her if colleagues attempted to overrule her.Influential pro-Rosebank voices suggested that senior ministers had toned down vocal support as the decision draws closer.They suggested this wasn't a sign that Rosebank would be vetoed, but because any obvious attempts to pressure the energy secretary might mean her final decision would be subject to a legal challenge. A number of MPs say they have heard conflicting claims - with both outcomes being predicted.What is clearer is that the government's decision will be controversial, whichever way it goes. There is a private and public battle playing out.Backers of the scheme argue approving it would provide an economic boost. The Conservatives also say it would enhance energy security.But oil is traded internationally – and the energy secretary has said approving the scheme will not help with immediate cost of living pressures. Rosebank would also be more polluting than Jackdaw, a gas field, which was approved last month.A fortnight ago, backers of the field were confident it would be approved.They believed the chancellor's language on energy bills at the Budget, coupled with the lack of political jeopardy that materialised from the approval of the Jackdaw gas field, had made their case stronger.The same group of MPs believe it would be difficult to reject Rosebank around the same time the prime minister is set to deliver a 10-year plan focused on reindustrialisation.The government has said oil and gas would be part of the energy mix for many years to come and sources in the trade union movement have suggested that if Rosebank doesn't go ahead, existing inward investment in the North Sea would be put at risk.While Labour's manifesto upon entering power in 2024 pledged not to "issue new licences to explore new fields", it does pledge to honour existing ones.In 2023, the then Conservative UK government granted a licence for Rosebank and a legal challenge followed.The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that the government had made the approval unlawfully, leaving the current Labour government to make a new decision on whether to give the go-ahead.The mood among some pro-Rosebank MPs changed this week, with several who back approval telling the BBC they were now worried it would be blocked.The BBC has spoken privately to Labour MPs involved in the debate, before the letter was sent to the prime minister, to get a sense of how divisive it is proving.One ministerial aide said: "There are quite a few of us who are considering our positions. I'm in that group. We want to see leadership on climate change."Another aide who said they might quit added: "There a group of us for whom we became Labour MPs because of climate change. It is the issue that motivated us into politics."Other aides – known in Westminster as parliamentary private secretaries – told the BBC they were opposed, but would stay in their jobs if it went ahead.Another said they thought there were increasing signs the prime minister would not be able to carry his party with him if the scheme was given the thumbs up.And another said the energy secretary might have to resign if it goes ahead, given her scepticism about the project.It has been reported in recent weeks that members of her team are encouraging opponents to make their feelings known. The BBC has been told the same.One MP, who backs Rosebank, said the behind-the-scenes operation had been so effective, the scheme was up in the air again.That has led to some anger at the energy secretary. One minister says: "Miatta has boxed herself in with how she's handled Rosebank. It's outrageous if she's encouraging MPs to speak up over Rosebank. We should get on and do it."Like the decision itself, the exact timeframe is unclear. But some opposition figures expect it mid-December.Whatever happens, it will be controversial and has already exposed splits in the Labour Party.

schema.headline: Nearly 100 Labour MPs including ministerial aides oppose Rosebank oil field

title: Gérard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged rape of actress in 2018, court rules
description: French film actor Gérard Depardieu is to stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, a Paris appeals court has confirmed.Arnould, w
body: French film actor Gérard Depardieu is to stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, a Paris appeals court has confirmed.Arnould, who was 22 at the time, had reported the alleged rape several days after going to his house in Paris to rehearse a play. She has waived her right to anonymity and her lawyer said Thursday's ruling was a "first" and the forthcoming trial would be historic. Depardieu, 77, had contested his indictment on two counts of rape. In a letter published in Le Figaro in 2023, Depardieu strongly denied Arnould's allegations, saying "there was never any coercion or violence between us". Depardieu was for decades a leading figure in French and international cinema for roles in Green Card, The Man in the Iron Mask and the Asterix films. He was awarded France's Légion d'honneur in 1996.But in recent years a series of allegations have been made against him over his conduct on film sets and elsewhere in the wake of France's #MeToo movement, known as balance ton porc (call out your pig).Last year, he was given an 18-month suspended jail term after he was found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set in Paris in May. He was also placed on the sex offenders register and ordered to pay compensation. He dropped his appeal against the ruling last week and offered "sincere apologies" for his behaviour on the set of director Jean Becker's 2021 film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters).Depardieu had been a friend of Charlotte Arnould's father and on 7 August 2018 she had gone to his home, where much of what happened was captured on the actor's own CCTV.Arnould's case was initially dismissed for insufficient evidence, but after she filed a civil complaint, a judicial investigation was opened in the summer of 2020. Speaking outside the Paris appeal court on Thursday, her lawyer Carine Durrieu Diebolt said the ruling was a victory for her client for whom it was "genuinely a relief".The appeal court said that while Depardieu should stand trial for what took place on that day, he would not be tried for a further alleged rape at a hotel six days later.Depardieu's lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski told reporters that court had partly ruled in his favour: "As soon as we get the ruling, we will look into the possibility of appealing to the Court of Cassation."Meanwhile, Depardieu is under a separate investigation alongside French author Michel Houellebecq for "allegations of a sexual nature".French authorities confirmed their inquiry last week, following reports of an alleged "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018.If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Gérard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged rape of actress in 2018, court rules

title: Princess of Wales visits Hugo Burge Foundation near Duns
description: Princess of Wales drops in on arts project in the BordersImage source, Press AssociationImage caption, The Princess of Wales - the Duchess of Rothesay
body: Princess of Wales drops in on arts project in the BordersImage source, Press AssociationImage caption, The Princess of Wales - the Duchess of Rothesay while in Scotland - met head gardener Toby Loveday during her visitByGiancarlo RinaldiSouth Scotland reporterThe Princess of Wales has been in the Scottish Borders to see the work of an arts organisation that is helping to support projects across the UK.It was her first engagement since two men were charged with trying to steal cufflinks and a clock from the royal couple's country home in Norfolk.The Hugo Burge Foundation (HBF) which has three bases in the region - one of them on the Marchmont Estate near Duns - carries the name of the internet entrepreneur and philanthropist who died in 2023 aged 51.The princess - who is known as the Duchess of Rothesay while in Scotland - got a glimpse of the work being carried out by the group.She was welcomed by Lucy Brown, HBF chief executive, and learned more about its work supporting creativity and craftsmanship.She also spent time talking to head gardener Toby Loveday and creative director James Fox during her time in the Borders.Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Lucy Brown (left) and James Fox took the royal visitor on a tourThe HBF offers grants, prizes, residencies and studio spaces to artists and craftspeople and provides funding to arts organisations and community groups.It also funds major public art projects with the goal of "permanently enriching Britain's cultural landscape".Established in 2022, last year it distributed more than £400,000 of grant funding to individuals, communities, organisations and projects.Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, The princess walked around the gardens on a cold but dry dayAcross its three locations, it offers a range of workspaces including a community pottery studio, a state-of-the-art silversmithing workshop, a printmaking studio, and a traditional chairmaking workshop.It also safeguards a nationally important collection of modern British art.On its main campus it offers funded residencies throughout the year and cares for a walled garden.In 2026, it opened Rhymer's Works, a new creative hub in the town of Earlston that offers subsidised studios and community spaces.Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, The Duchess of Rothesay talked with charcoal artist Tansy Lee Moir during her visitImage source, Press AssociationImage caption, The princess spent her afternoon at the south of Scotland siteImage source, Press AssociationImage caption, Artist Siobhan McLaughlin also spent some time with the royal guestImage source, Press AssociationImage caption, The princess tried her hand at some of the arts and crafts opportunities on offerImage source, Press AssociationImage caption, Artists got the opportunity to meet the princess during her stay

schema.headline: Princess of Wales visits Hugo Burge Foundation near Duns

title: New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause
description: The government and the EU have published the texts of two treaties agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.The treaties were published on Thur
body: The government and the EU have published the texts of two treaties agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.The treaties were published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.The deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay "reasonable and proportionate costs" to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal while Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay.The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the future of the UK-EU relationship.The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.Two of the three legal texts were released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.A new assessment of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country was also released. Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost the export of major agricultural commodities.The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements.""It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."A plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.The treaty text also contains finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules. The UK will be invited to attend European Commission meetings and expert groups as an observer, as well as taking part in emergency food security planning. However, the UK will not be given voting rights.Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, are detailed in the legislation.Such powers will enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny. Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week, the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

schema.headline: New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause

title: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds
description: Figure caption, Watch: BBC confronts German boat dealer Marvin ReuterByJessica ParkerBerlin correspondent and Tom BealBBC News InvestigationsA German
body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC confronts German boat dealer Marvin ReuterByJessica ParkerBerlin correspondent and Tom BealBBC News InvestigationsA German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police. Reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.The BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.Evidence has been gathered through the confessions of alleged accomplices and covert jail-cell recordings of an alleged gang chief - as well as the two deadly crossing attempts.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A press photo from 2021 - migrants in a boat from Marvin Reuter's firm (logo circled) At least 82 boats from Reuter's firm reached the English coast in just over two years to May, according to French investigations.There are also press photos dating back five years showing the MaReBoote logo on dinghies crowded with migrants.In 2021, Reuter told the Sun and Guardian he felt "frustrated" and "anxious" that his vessels had ended up in the hands of smugglers.There was no suggestion, at that time, that authorities suspected him of wrongdoing as a German detective reportedly told the Sun: "This would be like if somebody buys a Mercedes and does something in another country which is wrong. The Mercedes seller can't help that."It is not exactly clear when police suspicions were aroused.French prosecutor Samuel Finielz would not comment on the details of the investigation but confirmed the head of a German company is currently the subject of a European Arrest Warrant.The warrant was issued in May this year and relates to alleged offences dating back to December 2024.While selling boats is "perfectly legal" it becomes illegal, said Finielz, "when one is fully aware that they will be used by networks involved in illegal immigration or human trafficking".Case files we have seen say that German police had learned from UK authorities that 29% of detected crossings this year, up to the end of April, involved boats and/or engines linked to MaReBoote.In France, five other men have already been charged as part of the investigation - an Iranian, three Iraqis and a Syrian.In one of the two fatal incidents where Reuter's equipment is suspected to be involved, one of those who died was also Syrian.Suliman al Husein would have just turned 20 when he died, according to a birth date listed in the files.News reports at the time say he suffered a cardiac arrest after likely being crushed on a packed dinghy during a failed launch, west of Calais, in January 2025.He was the first migrant to die in the English Channel that year. His body was found on the floor of the boat which, investigators allege, bore the MaReBoote logo.Image caption, One night in May, French police stopped a car and seized boating equipment and fuel cansThe case against Reuter also stems from a chance arrest when French police pulled over a vehicle with German plates, near the northern port city of Boulogne-sur-Mer.The BMW, which was towing a trailer, was spotted overtaking another vehicle at speed in the early hours of a morning in May this year - police records say.Inside the car were two German nationals who - according to a subsequent search - were transporting jerry cans of fuel, a boat engine, pumps and a rolled up inflatable dinghy.The men claimed they had been paid up to €1,000-a-time (£830) to make several, similar drops to "foreigners" on the coast, interrogation records show."Of course I knew that it wasn't legal," one is said to have admitted under questioning. "The money made me turn a blind eye."Take a look at BBC Verify's UK migration tracker - the latest numbers on net migration, visas, asylum and small boatsBoth men, who have since been convicted for smuggling offences, allegedly implicated Marvin Reuter as the man who had hired and paid them for this work.Police files say both the BMW and the boat it was carrying had MaReBoote logos on them.Marvin Reuter was arrested in Germany in May and later released, pending extradition.On the day of his arrest, German police also seized more than 30 dinghies and 9,000 life jackets. Equipment which, we can now reveal, was allegedly linked to Reuter.The BBC was previously granted access to see this haul, held in a police warehouse at a secret location in western Germany.Image caption, Part of the haul of dinghies and life jackets shown to us by German policeMeanwhile, further evidence has been gleaned from the bugging of a jail cell of a suspected gang chief, who is being held in pre-trial detention in France.Recordings captured the inmate talking about buying nautical equipment from a German firm run by a man with Reuter's first name: Marvin - according to files we have seen.The MaReBoote company address was also discovered on the alleged smuggler's phone, the case files say.Image caption, We confronted Marvin Reuter at his company premises. We have blurred his face because of German privacy rulesWhen we confronted Reuter last month at his business in the town of Werne, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, he told us to leave and drove off.He then returned a short time later and said he was reporting us to the police. He did not answer our questions.We approached him in writing before and after this encounter including a detailed request for comment. In response to that request, he did not address the specific allegations but accused us of harassment.It is understood Reuter's lawyers have challenged his extradition, citing overcrowding in French prisons as one reason. Their client should face any allegations in Germany, they argue.Image caption, Reuter's firm is based in Werne, near DortmundIn Germany, it became explicitly illegal to aid smuggling to the UK at the end of last year after a prior BBC investigation exposed the country's role as a storage hub for gangs. Before then, some anti-smuggling laws in Germany had no longer applied to the UK because of Brexit.The raid that saw the seizure of equipment that was allegedly linked to Reuter marked the first time the new law had been used.Small boat crossings have dropped significantly in 2026, with British authorities citing law enforcement as a "key factor". However, illegal migration into Europe has also been falling.The UK National Crime Agency's (NCA) deputy director for organized immigration crime, Dan Cannatella-Barcroft, praised Germany's "commitment" to tackling people-smuggling but acknowledged the country would remain "an important piece of the puzzle".While a gap in the law has been closed, Germany's proximity to France, wider transport links and the fact that some of the Kurdish-dominated gangs are based there, means it is expected to stay as a transit point in the illegal small-boats trade.The "vast majority" of small boats equipment in the past few years has come through Germany, Cannatella-Barcroft told the BBC - much of it made in China and having been routed through Turkey.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds

title: Raheem Sterling: After court case how common is nitrous oxide in football?
description: It is known as laughing gas but the impact nitrous oxide can have on a professional footballer's body is anything but funny."I'm not going to name nam
body: It is known as laughing gas but the impact nitrous oxide can have on a professional footballer's body is anything but funny."I'm not going to name names but I have colleagues who know Premier League footballers who are no longer playing as a direct result of nitrous oxide [use]," said Dr David Nicholl.Nicholl, a clinical lead in neurology with Sandwell and West Birmingham NHS Trust, was speaking after former Manchester City, Chelsea, Liverpool and England forward Raheem Sterling was handed a suspended jail term after pleading guilty to dangerous driving.A key part of the case was that Sterling had been inhaling nitrous oxide from a balloon while driving. His Lamborghini was seen veering across a motorway and later crashed into a metal gate. Sterling, 31, was arrested at the scene and found with six gas canisters in his car.He disclosed to custody staff "he had a problem with nitrous oxide", the court was told.Defending Sterling, Jason Bartfeld KC said his client "recognised the various unhealthy coping mechanisms that brought him to this position" and that he has "sought to address" these in the "most positive and effective way and with some success".So, what is nitrous oxide, how does it affect those who take it and is its use more common in footballers than the wider population?Nitrous oxide's original use was as a sedative that healthcare providers like dentists could use to keep patients comfortable during procedures.It is now legally sold for catering, medical and industrial purposes, but is frequently used as a recreational drug and is commonly known as laughing gas.This can be abused by inhaling the gas via a balloon, leading to a short-term high causing symptoms such as brief euphoria, mild perceptual changes and uncontrollable laughter, external.Nitrous oxide also slows brain and body responses and can displace oxygen in the lungs and bloodstream, contributing to dizziness, confusion or fainting.It is thought long-term or excessive use can have disastrous effects on the body, from neurological harms to nerve and spinal cord damage which could lead to permanent disability.According to medical journal The Lancet, it is now the third most commonly used drug after cannabis and cocaine in the UK, with use highest among people aged 16–24 years.  It has been increasing in popularity as a recreational drug over the past decade.  This prompted it to be reclassified as a Class C drug in 2023 after a government consultation.BBC Sport has been told the abuse of so-called laughing gas has been widespread among professional footballers for a long time.Former player Drewe Broughton is now a human performance coach, working with Premier League footballers and clubs around the world.  He said laughing gas was seen by some as a release."I think the use of nitrous oxide is really common," he added."It's something that can be done in private. It's something that can be hidden. You can't smell it on their clothes or the breath. It's an underground thing."Broughton said he had been in the company of professional players when they had been using 'balloons'.   "I remember sitting in a players' house on the outskirts of Manchester, and these canisters were all over the floor," he added."I was from a world where people drank or they gambled or went to pubs and nightclubs. That was my first exposure to it."Broughton has developed an app to help tackle issues with mental health and under-performance in football.  He said the reasons to use nitrous oxide had always been there: pressure on players to perform leaves them searching for an escape.  But Broughton has concerns about the toll nitrous oxide can take.  "I don't think there's the same awareness around nitrous oxide and damage to the body as there would be around alcohol or other drugs," he said.BBC Sport has been told that some footballers see laughing gas as an alternative to harder substances because it does not stay in the body's system for more than a few hours.Luci Hanmer, who works with Lancashire drugs and alcohol support charity 'We Are With You', said a substance like nitrous oxide was hard to detect.   She said: "Anything that you're inhaling, the effects that you're going to feel happen very soon."So if you are looking for that escapism, the effects are going to be quick.  "Once ingested, it doesn't last very long within your body compared to some of the other substances which can be detected for quite a number of days."So if you're getting a drugs test the next day for example, that won't show up."Former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha said more support was needed, particularly for players like Sterling who break through young.Sterling made his debut for Liverpool and England at just 17 - before going on to win four Premier League titles at Manchester City and 82 caps for his country, including the Euro 2020 final at Wembley."Look at what's happened to Raheem," he said. "Look at how this led to this moment, a moment which I'm sure he's hugely embarrassed about, because I'm sure he can see how dangerous that was to not just his life, but the lives of so many people who are on the road at the same time."But I just don't feel like football is in a position where they think it's important to support people who have issues with nitrous oxide."The BBC Radio 5 live pundit said the use of nitrous oxide in professional footballing circles was very common.  "I think the difference from when I was younger is that people would openly party in certain places," he said."Now they party where they're harder to spot. That's why you don't really see on a week-to-week basis now the scandal of somebody that's been out drinking."The players are doing it, but it's more sophisticated in terms of how they do it, the locations, and this is an example here with nitrous oxide."Neurologist Dr Nicholl has been working with patients who have abused nitrous oxide for years and issued a warning to others."It certainly is being used by footballers, but it's pretty much the worst thing that you want to be using if you're a professional sportsperson," he said."It damages your spinal cord and the spinal cord is a bit like an electrical cable, where the insulation - the outside of that cable - gets stripped away."So what patients will complain of is difficulty with feeling on their hands or feet, or unable to walk at all.  "So, in effect, it's like a spinal cord injury. But they can also get blood clots, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary emboli, and some patients have died."If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line website.

schema.headline: Raheem Sterling: After court case how common is nitrous oxide in football?

title: Andy Burnham joined by former PMs for Widdecombe service
description: Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and a number of previous prime ministers attended the service ByBritta Zeltm
body: Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and a number of previous prime ministers attended the service ByBritta Zeltmann and Cameron WeldonDevonUpdated 1 hour agoAndy Burnham was joined by former prime ministers at a memorial service for the late politician Ann Widdecombe.The Service of Remembrance at Westminster Cathedral was held on Thursday afternoon, with eulogies delivered and a choir performance. Hundreds of guests attended, with David Cameron, Liz Truss, Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak among them. Bishop James Curry, the Auxiliary Bishop of Westminster, led the service after the Archbishop of Westminster, Richard Moth, was taken to hospital earlier.Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Reform UK's chairman Lee Anderson, deputy leader Richard Tice and leader Nigel Farage were among those at the serviceMoth, who is the head of the Catholic Church in England and Wales, underwent tests after he "felt unwell", Westminster Diocese said.Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, former Conservative MP Philip Hammond, and Speaker of the House of Commons Sir Lindsay Hoyle also attended.Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Prime Minister Andy Burnham shakes hands with former prime minister Rishi Sunak at the serviceThe Prime Minister was later seen leaving the cathedral with former prime ministers Rishi Sunak and Boris Johnson. Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK's justice spokeswoman, was found dead at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon, on 9 July, aged 78.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Politicians past and present gathered for the service remembering Ann WiddecombeJoshua Kerry, 28, of Byrley Road, Rotherham, South Yorkshire, was charged with her murder.A trial before a High Court judge is scheduled for 8 June, and a plea and case management hearing on 29 January.Widdecombe's family announced plans for a public memorial service following her death.Widdecombe served as Conservative MP for Maidstone and the Weald in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Archbishop of Westminster Richard Moth is undergoing tests after being taken to hospitalImage source, Press AssociationImage caption, Prime Minister Andy Burnham leaves Westminster Cathedral with former prime ministers Rishi Sunak and Boris Johnson following the serviceImage source, Press AssociationImage caption, Former Conservative leader Sir Iain Duncan Smith attended the serviceShe became a member of Reform in 2019 as a party spokeswoman.Away from politics, she appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing in 2010 and was a runner-up on Celebrity Big Brother eight years later.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham joined by former PMs for Widdecombe service

title: BBC launches partnership with Met Office for weather coverage
description: The BBC has said it will offer more regional, digital and 10-day weather forecasts under a new partnership with the Met Office, which begins on Thursd
body: The BBC has said it will offer more regional, digital and 10-day weather forecasts under a new partnership with the Met Office, which begins on Thursday.The collaboration, announced last year, aims to bring together the Met Office's weather and climate intelligence with the BBC's journalism and reach, the broadcaster said.Director general Matt Brittin said the partnership would mean "serving our audiences with the most accurate, reliable and helpful weather service we can".But the launch comes during a savings drive at the corporation, which has seen some other weather services and bulletins dropped as part of wider cuts.The new Met Office partnership is unrelated to the cuts and was announced last July, before the BBC embarked on its latest round of savings. The BBC said the partnership includes:A new hourly forecast on the BBC News website and app covering 10 days, with improved medium-range forecastsMet Office severe weather warning notifications via the BBC Weather appMore local and more digital weather reports, and more forecasts fronted by local weather presentersMore "content collaboration on BBC and Met Office channels" using Met Office expertise, and helping to explain weather and climateThere will also be Met Office branding on weather reports, and a new BBC weather centre based in the agency's headquarters in Exeter.Brittin said the collaboration would involve "turning science into stories and helping audiences make informed decisions with our forecasts".Separately, the BBC has dropped or shortened a number of national television and radio weather bulletins in recent weeks, as the corporation continues to work towards a £500m savings target.Some weekend and late-night forecasts have been dropped from the TV schedules, with regional presenters instead now delivering a UK-wide weather outlook during their presenting slots. Listeners have also complained about programmes such as Radio 4's PM no longer delivering a full weather bulletin, with presenter Evan Davis instead reading a short summary and directing listeners to the BBC website for a more detailed forecast. The BBC said it was changing its weather team to better serve digital platforms, in line with audience research and changing consumption habits. The corporation said more users are accessing weather information via the BBC's app, website and social platforms, as the number of people relying on broadcast bulletins declines.A spokesman for the corporation said: "The BBC is committed to providing a world-class public service for weather forecasting and information across our platforms."As we announced in July, we are making changes to the way we deliver weather information as more people are turning to mobile and the website for their weather forecasts. We also recognise that people want more local forecasts, along with the national picture, to help them plan their coming days more accurately."As such we are providing more digital and localised forecasts, as well as ensuring we still have appropriate national weather bulletins across the TV and radio."BBC Radio 4's Today programme, BBC Breakfast and the weekday editions of BBC One's News at Six will retain their usual national weather forecasts.

schema.headline: BBC launches partnership with Met Office for weather coverage

title: Davis Cup Finals 2026: Great Britain beat Germany to reach semi-finals
description: GB win decider to reach Davis Cup semi-finalsFigure caption, Highlights: Skupski and Patten win thrilling doubles match to seal Davis Cup winByElizabe
body: GB win decider to reach Davis Cup semi-finalsFigure caption, Highlights: Skupski and Patten win thrilling doubles match to seal Davis Cup winByElizabeth BotcherbyBBC Sport journalistUpdated 38 minutes agoGreat Britain advanced to the semi-finals of the Davis Cup for the first time since 2019 as Henry Patten and Neal Skupski won a decisive doubles tie against third seeds Germany in Bologna.Patten and Skupski, playing together for the first time since announcing their doubles partnership for the 2027 season, proved too clinical for Kevin Krawietz and Tim Puetz.They converted two break points and saved five in the first set, before overturning a mini-break in the tie-break to win 6-2 7-6 (8-6).Skupski was involved in a Davis Cup quarter-final loss playing alongside Joe Salisbury against the same German doubles pair in December 2021 - a defeat that was in his mind as Thursday's decider progressed."I thought about that match during the match today and I was determined not to let that happen again," Skupski told BBC Radio 5 Live."No matter what was happening today, we weren't going to come off the court very easily with a loss."World number one Alexander Zverev had earlier sent the tie to its full distance by defeating British number one Arthur Fery in straight sets to cancel out Cameron Norrie's three-set victory over Jan-Lennard Struff.Great Britain's semi-final is scheduled for Saturday and Leon Smith's team will discover their next opponents later on Thursday when Spain meet Austria in the last of the four quarter-finals.Defending champions Italy will play Czech Republic in Friday's first semi-final.Smith will step down as captain at the end of the tournament and Great Britain retain hopes of a second victory under his leadership, following the most recent of their 10 Davis Cup successes in 2015."I felt the same sort of pressure, nerves and butterflies beforehand and during the matches," said Smith, who has been captain since 2010."You sit for a long time in that chair on your own on a day like this, a lot of thoughts go through your head and one of the things I kept reminding myself is how much of a privilege it is to be in this situation."I loved it but, more importantly, I'm thrilled for the guys. They've committed so well to this, they've been to a few different places over the past 18 months to get to this opportunity and I'm delighted they've got to the final four now."Norrie wins but defeat for FeryFigure caption, Highlights: Norrie beats Struff in three sets to give GB lead in Davis CupWorld number 52 Norrie had got Great Britain off to the perfect start with a three-set win against Struff, a player 13 places above him in the world rankings.The left-hander raced through the first set in just 23 minutes but a break late in the second set by Struff forced a decider.The key moment came at 2-2 in the final set when Norrie saved four break points to hold serve, after which he won 12 of the next 14 points to complete a 6-3 3-6 6-2 victory.Norrie's success meant a win for Fery against Zverev, a two-time major champion in 2026, would have been enough to secure Great Britain's passage through to the last four.However, as he did in their Wimbledon semi-final in July, Zverev proved too strong for 24-year-old Fery and ended as a 6-3 6-2 winner.Figure caption, Highlights: Zverev beats Fery to draw Germany level in Davis CupPatten and Skupski have found themselves unusually in the spotlight over the past week following the former's "ruthless" split from Harri Heliovaara in favour of joining forces with his compatriot next season.While their partnership is in its infancy, there were few signs of teething problems as they extended their Davis Cup record as a pair to 3-0.Patten's pinpoint returns and sharp reactions at the net coupled with Skupski's impressive serving proved too strong for Krawietz and Puetz, who were left to rue missed opportunities.In a sticky opening service game, Patten double-faulted on the opening point and faced a break point, while Skupski saved four in game seven of the opening set.Neither pair earned a break point in the second set, with the British duo dropping just five points on serve.Trailing 3-1 in what turned out to be a thrilling tie-break, they fought back to lead 6-5 before closing out the win at the second opportunity."It doesn't feel like the end of the season for those two because they've just paired up," Smith said. "There's been a buoyancy in their practice sessions because it's a new start."They were brilliant today. You don't know if you're going to get a match or not [as doubles players] but I saw them 20 minutes before their match and you could just see they were delighted to get this opportunity and that gave them a huge lift."

schema.headline: Davis Cup Finals 2026: Great Britain beat Germany to reach semi-finals

title: Qatar Grand Prix: George Russell says Max Verstappen's criticism of him is 'quite amusing'
description: Asked whether he wanted to pursue reconciliation with Dutchman Verstappen, Russell said: "We're all competitors out there. There's no right or wrong w
body: Asked whether he wanted to pursue reconciliation with Dutchman Verstappen, Russell said: "We're all competitors out there. There's no right or wrong way about the mentality everybody has."We are all different in many regards and you don't need to agree with one another. I'm not looking to be best mates with anybody on the grid. I am just working and looking and fighting to win. Simple as that."British driver Russell said he had learned lessons from the incident in Vegas, which is the latest in a series of flashpoints between himself and four-time champion Verstappen dating back several years, and he might change how open he is with the media in future."It's all avoidable at the end of the day," Russell said. "It's all a bit unnecessary. It's not something I am looking to continue. I am not looking to have a poor relationship with people. That's not really the kind of person I am."There are lessons to be taken from these situations. Maybe I am just too open and honest with the media. I need to remember I'm talking to a camera that is broadcasting to millions of people. That's the biggest takeaway."It is not a war of words off track. I maybe have been guilty of being too open and honest when I speak with you guys."I feel like I have a good relationship with the media and I sometimes forget I am not talking to one person - I am talking to millions of people on the television."That good relationship has probably hindered me a bit and that is life lessons. I respect Max immensely for his driving talent and what he has achieved on track."

schema.headline: Qatar Grand Prix: George Russell says Max Verstappen's criticism of him is 'quite amusing'

title: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
description: One aircraft was meant to depart London for Orlando this morning, while another was meant to arrive from Cape Town this evening.The suspension has als
body: One aircraft was meant to depart London for Orlando this morning, while another was meant to arrive from Cape Town this evening.The suspension has also affected Pakistan International Airlines, which had been leasing aircraft and crews from Norse Atlantic.PIA was forced to cancel services from London to Islamabad and from Manchester to Lahore last night.In a statement on social media, PIA said all UK flights from today would be operated by aircraft from its own fleet.Londoner Fred was due to fly to Cape Town with Norse Atlantic next week for a friend's wedding, but has decided to change his plans."Yesterday the exact same flight I was going to get was cancelled, so I was worried" he told the BBC's Your Voice. "I sent an email to Norse and have had nothing back".He decided to rebook with a different airline, which cost him an extra £1,000.Another traveller, Claire from Herefordshire, is currently on holiday in South Africa with her daughter."We are due to fly home on Sunday and are now looking at a really expensive flight back," she said."We have tried contacting Norse but have been given an automated response saying someone will get back to us within three business days."Norse Atlantic Airways was set up in 2021 as a low-cost long-haul carrier.It entered the market as a successor to Norwegian, which withdrew from long haul routes as a result of the Covid pandemic.But it has struggled to make money, and its problems worsened this year, as fuel prices rocketed due to the war in Iran.Unlike many other European carriers, Norse Atlantic does not hedge its fuel bills by buying supplies in advance at fixed prices.This left it fully exposed when prices soared, with the cost of fuel roughly doubling at one point. Prices remain significantly higher than they were before the conflict began.In the first half of the year Norse Atlantic made a loss of $94.6m.In a statement to the Oslo Stock Exchange on Wednesday, the airline said its financial situation was critical, and it needed to find short term funding to continue its operations.After suspending flights, the company said it was in discussions with investors regarding a possible takeover that "would include a financing solution".However, it said if short term funding could not be found quickly, "it is the Board's intention to file for bankruptcy".Norse Atlantic had been looking for a buyer since July.Its potential collapse follows the failure of Spirit Airlines in May. The US-based low cost carrier was another airline left exposed when jet fuel prices soared, as US airlines typically do not hedge their purchases.If Norse Atlantic were to fold, it would be another major setback for the low-cost long-haul model, which has typically proved popular with passengers but difficult to sustain financially, especially on transatlantic routes. Additional reporting by Rozina Sini

schema.headline: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse

title: Golf: Nick Faldo urges LIV stars to 'chip in' for unpaid firms
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Sir Nick Faldo's comments follow a BBC Sport investigationByTom GrundyBBC Sport senior journalistSir Nick Fal
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Sir Nick Faldo's comments follow a BBC Sport investigationByTom GrundyBBC Sport senior journalistSir Nick Faldo has suggested, external those who financially benefited from LIV Golf should "chip in and take care of" businesses owed money by the Saudi-backed tour.His comments have been welcomed by UK companies still waiting to be paid.A BBC Sport investigation found that LIV paid millions to players and executives in the weeks before filing for bankruptcy, while bills from suppliers were already overdue.Faldo - arguably Britain's greatest golfer - said the controversial breakaway tour risked "ruining the small businesses that help make their events possible"."British suppliers who cleaned venues and kept events running are still owed hundreds of thousands of pounds," added the six-time major winner."Maybe if those on and off the golf course feel they were overcompensated for their worth, they should chip in and take care of this matter."Since the investigation was published, more firms have contacted us about money they are owed by LIV.They include sports communications company Soapbox, which works with the likes of Anthony Joshua and Luke Littler and is owed tens of thousands of pounds."I'm incredibly grateful to Sir Nick Faldo for speaking out," said Krissi Foskett, whose cleaning company BD365 Clean is £75,225 out of pocket."For the last couple of months I've felt powerless. Having someone of his standing recognise the injustice of what's happening to businesses like ours genuinely means a lot."Sir Nick's suggestion that those who have benefited financially could contribute towards paying the outstanding suppliers is something I wholeheartedly welcome."LIV Golf has not responded to requests for comment on the original investigation or Faldo's remarks.In August, chief executive Scott O'Neil said he hoped the tour would be able to pay its suppliers."What I would say to them is we're doing everything we can to make sure we can do right by them and the work they committed."I come from a family of entrepreneurs, a family of small business entrepreneurs and know the challenge."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Scott O'Neil (right) took over from Greg Norman (left) as LIV chief executive in January 2025Faldo's one-time on-course rival, Greg Norman, was chief executive of LIV Golf until last year.Court filings show the Australian received $9.4m (£7.2m) in settlement and bonus payments in September 2025.His successor, O'Neil, received a retention bonus of $6.4m (£4.9m) in June this year.In September, Norman told The Real Deal with Bob Philion podcast that he was proud of bringing private equity into the sport."In a period of basically 2021 to now, close to $8bn (£6.1bn) has been brought into the game of golf," he said.Responding to those comments, Faldo told BBC Sport: "Eight billion dollars is 8,000 million dollars. If that is a full six years, that is approximately $3.6m (£2.8m) a day."Before LIV filed for bankruptcy, seven executives received $15.6m (£11.9m) in retention payments, with further bonuses also paid. "Now they risk ruining the small businesses that help make their events possible."BBC Sport has contacted Norman for a response.Figure caption, LIV Golf's bankruptcy and its debt to British businesses'I'm not the one who should feel ashamed'Companies still owed money include Global Infusion Group, which provided catering at July's LIV Golf UK event and is awaiting £321,671 - which was due on 7 August.Public records also list more than £3,000 owed to Goodysphere, a family-run Yorkshire firm that provides a sensory bus designed to help autistic children who may find busy events overwhelming.Just $2m (£1.5m) has been proposed so far by LIV's Saudi owners to pay unsecured creditors, leaving many smaller companies unsure whether they will receive anything at all."I've spent months questioning myself, feeling ashamed that our financial difficulties might be perceived as poor management," said Foskett."When I look at the billions poured into LIV Golf and the millions reportedly paid to executives, whilst I was personally climbing in and out of skips to meet their zero-waste policy, I've come to realise that I'm not the one who should feel ashamed."We didn't invest in LIV Golf. We didn't gamble on its success. We simply went to work."Scott O'Neil talks about understanding small businesses. Sir Nick Faldo is standing up for them. Right now, I know whose words mean more to me."

schema.headline: Golf: Nick Faldo urges LIV stars to 'chip in' for unpaid firms
